title: Pooling
objectives: Write max and average pooling, and say what each throws away.

screens.title: Max pooling and average pooling
screens.prose: What you did is **max pooling**: keep the largest value in each window. **Average pooling** keeps the mean instead. With 2 by 2 windows both halve each side, and both tolerate a small shift a little, as the left windows did.
screens.question: What is the top-left value of the average-pooled map?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Average the four values of the top-left window.

byKey.max: That is the max-pooled value. Average pooling takes the mean.
byKey.sum: That is the sum. Divide by the 4 values.

screens.title: Where the gradient goes
screens.prose: Backward, a max-pooled value passed on one input and ignored the other three. A gradient of 1 arrives at the top-left pooled value, 4.
screens.question: Tap the input cell that receives it.

hints.text: Which value did the window keep?

feedback.correct: Only the 4 at row 1, column 0 moved the output, so only it gets the gradient.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which input decided the pooled value?

byKey.spread: You spread it over the window, as average pooling would. Max pooling passes it to the winner alone.
byKey.r1c2: The 3 lost to the 4; nudging it changes nothing, so its gradient is 0.

explain.text: Nudge the 4 and the output moves with it; nudge any other cell of the window and nothing happens. So the gradient is 1 at the 4 and 0 at the rest.

screens.title: Spreading it evenly
screens.prose: Average pooling used every input with weight $\tfrac14$. A gradient of 2 arrives at the top-left average-pooled value.
screens.question: What gradient does each of the four inputs receive?

hints.text: The weight of each input in the mean is $\tfrac14$.
Chain rule: incoming gradient times the weight.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each input entered the mean with weight $\tfrac14$.

byKey.all: Each input moved the mean by a quarter of its own change. Multiply by $\tfrac14$.
byKey.quarter: That is the weight. Multiply it by the incoming gradient, 2.

explain.text: $\partial y/\partial x = \tfrac14$ for each input, so each gets $2 \times \tfrac14 = 0.5$; the four shares add back to 2.

screens.title: "Pooling makes it shift-invariant"
screens.prose: A colleague says max pooling makes a network ignore where a pattern sits, so a chart shifted by a day reads the same. You saw the map moved one pixel.

state.caption: The moved map and its pooled values.

screens.question: What is true of max pooling?

options.text: It tolerates some shifts; others move a maximum into the next window
The pooled map never changes under a one-pixel shift
options.why: You saw two of four pooled values change when the 6 slid out of its window.

options.text: It is invariant to any shift smaller than the window
options.why: A shift of one pixel is smaller than the 2-pixel window, and the output still changed.

options.text: Average pooling is invariant where max pooling is not
options.why: The averages changed too: each right-hand window now holds different values.

hints.text: Which values crossed a window edge?
The 6 moved from column 3 out of the map.

feedback.correct: A shift that keeps each maximum inside its window changes nothing; one that crosses a window edge does.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look back at the bottom-right window.

byKey.b: You took the claim on trust. The moved map pooled to $(4, 3; 3, 5)$ instead of $(4, 2; 3, 6)$.

explain.text: The 4 and the 3 stayed in their windows, so those pooled values held. The 6 crossed a window edge and was lost. Pooling buys tolerance to some small shifts, not invariance.

screens.title: A tie in the window
screens.prose: A window holds $(3, 3; 1, 0)$: two maxima. A gradient of 1 arrives. The convention in this course, as in `np.argmax`, sends it to the first maximum in row-major order: along the top row first.
screens.question: Tap the cell that receives the gradient.

hints.text: Flatten the window row by row.
The first 3 is the top-left cell.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the window row by row, left to right.

byKey.r1c2: That is the second 3. The first one met in row-major order wins.
byKey.split: Splitting it would be another convention. Here one cell takes it all.

explain.text: `np.argmax` of the flattened window $(3, 3, 1, 0)$ is 0, the top-left cell. Either choice gives a valid gradient: on a tie the max is not differentiable, so a library picks one and the tests say which.

screens.title: What pooling keeps and throws away
screens.prose: For windows of $s$ by $s$ at stride $s$: $$y_{ij} = \max_{0 \le a, b < s} x_{si+a,\, sj+b} \quad \text{or} \quad y_{ij} = \frac{1}{s^2}\sum_{a, b} x_{si+a,\, sj+b}.$$ Backward, max pooling routes each gradient to the winner; average pooling spreads it as $1/s^2$ each.
screens.question: Which pooling remembers where in its window the largest value was?

options.why: It keeps the value, not its place: the 4 could have sat in any corner.
The mean mixes all four values and forgets their places too.
The output has one number per window and no position.

feedback.correct: One number per window: the position inside it is gone.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What does the output hold for each window?

explain.text: Max pooling throws away the three smaller values and the winner’s position; average pooling throws away the spread and every position. Both shrink the map by $s^2$.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np


def maxpool_backward(x, size, dout):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    dout = np.asarray(dout, dtype=float)
    dx = np.zeros_like(x)
    for i in range(dout.shape[0]):
        for j in range(dout.shape[1]):
            win = x[i * size:(i + 1) * size, j * size:(j + 1) * size]
            a, b = np.unravel_index(np.argmax(win), win.shape)
            dx[i * size + a, j * size + b] += dout[i, j]
    return dx

mutants.source:
import numpy as np


def maxpool_backward(x, size, dout):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    dout = np.asarray(dout, dtype=float)
    dx = np.zeros_like(x)
    for i in range(dout.shape[0]):
        for j in range(dout.shape[1]):
            win = x[i * size:(i + 1) * size, j * size:(j + 1) * size]
            a, b = divmod(int(np.argmax(win)), size)
            dx[i * size + b, j * size + a] += dout[i, j]
    return dx
mutants.symptom: Row and column inside the window are swapped.

screens.title: The worst day of each week
screens.prose: A risk report shows the worst daily loss of each week. Ten days of desk P&L in £ are shown; a loss is minus the P&L. Taking the largest loss in each run of 5 days is max pooling over time with a window of 5.
screens.question: What is the worst daily loss in week 2, in £?

hints.text: A loss is minus the P&L.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Turn each P&L into a loss, then take the largest in days 6 to 10.

byKey.max-pnl: That is the best day of the week. The worst loss is the largest of the losses.
byKey.average: That is average pooling of the losses. The report wants the worst day.
byKey.week1: That is week 1. Week 2 is days 6 to 10.

explain.text: Week 2’s losses are $60, 410, -150, 220, -30$, so the pooled value is £410. Like max pooling, the report keeps the worst value and forgets which day it fell on.

ideas: Max pooling keeps the largest value of each window; average pooling keeps the mean. With $s$ by $s$ windows at stride $s$ both divide each side by $s$.
Backward, max pooling sends each gradient to the window’s winner (the first, on a tie) and 0 elsewhere; average pooling gives each input $1/s^2$ of it.
Both throw away positions inside the window; max pooling also drops the smaller values. They tolerate some small shifts, not all: a maximum that crosses a window edge changes the output.

formula.name: Max and average pooling
formula.tex: y_{ij} = \max_{a, b < s} x_{si+a,\, sj+b}, \qquad \bar y_{ij} = \tfrac{1}{s^2}\sum_{a, b < s} x_{si+a,\, sj+b}

summary.trap: "Pooling makes a network shift-invariant": a one-pixel shift moved the 6 out of its window and changed two of four pooled values.
